content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of domain generalization for tiny neural networks. It finds that knowledge distillation with strong augmentations can imrove DG for tiny neural network more than other DG methods developed for larger models. Also it propose a scalable method for creating DG datasets, called DOmain Shift in COntext (DOSCO). It clusters the images with Places features to synthesize domain labels.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
* The paper is well written and easy to follow. 
* The problem is well motivated.


### Weaknesses
* The proposed method is too simple and not innovative. Doing KD with augmentation for OOD is very natural for the problem. It doesn't address the difference of DG between tiny and larger neural network.  
* The paper doesn't have much insight about why the proposed method works better than previous sota methods on tiny neural networks.
* The proposed DOSCO dataset is not really relevant to the problem itself. It has nothing tailored to the tiny neural networks.
* For the synthetic domain labels in the DOSCO, images with each class is clustered separately. Does that mean there is no consistency among domains across different classes in one dataset?  In this case, the synthetic domain label is more like "sub-class" instead of "domain".

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies on-device domain generalization, which is DG for tiny neural networks. Authors claimed that existing DG approaches are not suitable for on-device DG, hence they find that knowledge distillation brings significant improvements to their datasets. To this end, they propose an out-of-distribution KD (OKD) to add another regularization (KL-div between augmented teacher and student datasets) to the original KD loss to address this problem. Then, authors claim that existing DG evaluation is not appropriate, and they propose DOSCO to construct a DG evaluation system based on MIT Places dataset. Experiments are done on their benchmark and show the effectiveness of OKD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

1. The study domain is interesting: the application of DG on tiny neural networks.
2. The method (OOD KD) brings significant improvements to their benchmarks.\
3. This paper is written well.

### Weakness

1. Novelty. The novelty is limited. The key technical contribution is OOD-KD (OKD), which merely adds a regularization term to the original KD loss to regularize the KL-divergence between augmented teacher and student data. This approach is pretty ad-hoc as they assume that the feature spaces for teacher and student are the same, which could not be the real case in IoT devices since one of the most crucial factors in IoT is the feature heterogeneity. Thus, I doubt the realistic value of this algorithm. In addition to its applicability, this approach is not novel for ICLR.
2. Motivation. The study of on-device DG is interesting, but I doubt the motivation of this application. If computational resources are limited for small IoT devices, then why not just use traditional (non-deep) machine learning algorithms? We can also use KNN, SVM, and random forest for machine learning tasks and they will certainly consume less computation resources than neural networks. Plus, this paper does not show the comparison of traditional DG vs deep DG algorithms. The parameters of tiny neural networks are much larger than traditional SVM or RFs, making it easier to overfit than them. There are tons of existing DG algorithms for traditional learning, which authors did not cite or compare. Therefore, the motivation of this paper is neither natural nor realistic.
And, to my best knowledge, the gap between ID and OOD is large, it is common sense. Thus, table 1 does not further justify the need for on-device domain generalization: the gap for ResNet is also large, not only tiny nets. And the ID-OOD gap is not dependent on network size.
3. The construction of DOSCO is interesting, but not reasonable. Why just use Places dataset to extract contextual information? There is a lack of motivation, interpretation, and theoretical guarantee: why is this dataset enough for all CV tasks? I truly do not think this is the right way to perform construction or validation on DG tasks. Besides, authors mentioned that DomainBed is widely used as DG benchmarks, then why not use it for experiments? I believe solely reliance on Places will introduce certain bias towards evaluation and even make it unfair.
4. In page 4, the claim that "existing datasets are limited in diversity xxx most are based on image style changes", are not right. In DomainBed, not every dataset is for style changes, such as CMNIST and TerraIncognia, which are NOT style changes. Then, why not use these datasets for evaluation, and instead, manipulate your own datasets? Besides, why not use the much larger WILDs datasets for evaluation, which is also not for style changes?
5. There are no theoretical guarantees that this OKD algorithm will converge or lead to satisfying performance. Moreover, I find this algorithm is highly dependent on the augmentation techniques: failing to choose the right augmentation techniques will lead to bad performance. Plus, this algorithm only works for image datasets, while there are more application domains than CV tasks for IoT devices, such as forecasting, time series, and more. Thus, this algorithm is not general.
6. There are also no ablation experiments on the importance of data augmentations.
7. The experimental datasets in this paper are very small, compared to existing datasets. Thus, it fails to justify the effectiveness of this approach.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Most of the writings are good, with sound expressions.
Reproducibility: not reproducible since there are no codes and datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review: Concisely, this idea of on-device DG is interesting, but authors should think about it more naturally and more reasonably. The current form is not ready for ICLR publications due to lack of motivation, low technical novelty, and theoretical guarantees.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a simple but efficient method - OKD, which utilizes the idea of the knowledge distillation to solve the domain generalization problem for the tiny neural networks. It introduces another distillation loss for out-of-distribution data during training. Besides, this paper also gives a novel method – DOSCO, to synthesize the domain generalization datasets with broader categories and a broader spectrum of domain shift by extracting contextual information in images and clustering to induce the labels. Further experiments have proved the proposed OKD can give better improvements over other KD methods and performs competitive compared to strong domain generalization methods for solving on-device domain generalization. At the same time, it shows that the proposed DOSCO is also scalable when building domain generalization datasets through the creating procedures and the results on this benchmark.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The idea of OKD is interesting, and performs well on domain generalization for tiny neural networks. The idea of DOSCO is novel and scalable, which can be used in domain generalization and facilitates the development of the research in this filed in the future.
2) The experimental results and ablation studies are solid and adequate to verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
3) This paper is well-written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
1) For the OOD Data Generator, this paper has compared some augmentation methods and demonstrate the reason to choose the combination of CutMix and Mixup. But the concrete reasons should be given by formula with more analysis through experiments. At the same time, some other transformation methods, such as Color Jittering can be added for a complete and further exploration.
2) For some downstream high-level vision tasks, such as object detection, semantic segmentation and so on, it is necessary for the paper to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed OKD method, and it would be better if some related experiments could be conducted to verify the idea.
3) Some of works presented in Related Work Section in the paper are suggested to introduce in detail for better understanding the previous works and the contributions of this work.
4) I wonder if DOSCO-2k dataset will be publicly available.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is well-written and the whole idea and the method description is clear.
Quality: The quality of the main paper is relatively high. Some suggestions in Strength and Weaknesses part can be referred to further polish the paper.
Novelty: It is novel of the whole idea of this paper. Although the idea of the proposed OKD is simple, it is quite efficient and scalable for on-device domain adaption problems. Another DOSCO benchmark is also novel for creating domain generalization datasets.
Reproducibility: The method proposed in this paper is easy to implement, and as illustrated in the paper, the code and models will be released, thus there is no concern about the reproducibility of this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of this paper is novel and effective, the overall framework seems to be simple, interesting and perform well according to the abundant experimental results. Some of my concerns have illustrated in the Strength and Weaknesses part, but it does not affect the evaluation of this work. I tend to accept this paper for ICLR 2023 and expects the further works in this filed and the concrete solutions of the problems presented in Section 6 in this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a simple method to improve domain generalization (DG) for on-device neural networks without increasing the inference cost. In detail, the student network (target network) is trained to mimic the teacher (larger) network’s prediction with respect to the synthetic out-of-distribution (OoD) input in a knowledge distillation manner. Furthermore, a dataset, called DOmain Shift in COntext (DOSCO) is established and can be applied to broad data at scale without much human effort.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper is well written and easy to follow.
2. The task setting is interesting and important to the research community.
3. Intriguing observations, such as performance declines significantly for tiny models, especially on OOD data.
4. Details of the datasets and experiments are provided.

Weakness:

Approach:
1. I am fine with each component of the proposed method, named out-of-distribution knowledge distillation (OKD) is not new, such as minimizing KL divergence between the output of the student and teacher, data generator (data augmentation). However, the proposed method is not designed specifically for OoD. It can be also adapted in an I.I.D setting, which makes it weak well-motivated, and less important to me. In addition, I cannot agree with the OoD data generator, such as Gaussian noise, Jigsaw, and mixup variants can generate high-quality OoD data. According to Figure 4, most of the generated images look like in-domain data.
2. It is not clear whether the performance gains in Tables 2 and 3 comes from the data generation or the KD loss of distilling teachers’ knowledge to students. More ablation studies are recommended. 

Dataset:
1. The dataset size is too small, compared with current DG benchmarks. 
2. As I mentioned above, the proposed synthetic data generator tends to not be able to generate OoD data. 
3. Also, compared with real-world datasets which contain both diversity shift and correlation shift [1], the proposed dataset cannot match the high-quality of them, and is not ideal for real-world application. 

[1] Ye, Nanyang, et al. "Ood-bench: Benchmarking and understanding out-of-distribution generalization datasets and algorithms." (CVPR2022).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity looks good to me, but the quality of the dataset and the novelty of the method need to be improved. See the questions above.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is interesting and easy to follow, but there are some issues with both the method and dataset. To me, the work needs a deep pass on them before being published.

content.title: On-Device Domain Generalization
content.TL;DR: A systematic study on how to improve domain generalization for tiny neural networks
content.abstract: We present a systematic study of domain generalization (DG) for tiny neural networks, a problem that is critical to on-device machine learning applications but has been overlooked in the literature where research has been focused on large models only. Tiny neural networks have much fewer parameters and lower complexity, and thus should not be trained the same way as their large counterparts for DG applications. We find that knowledge distillation is a strong candidate for solving the problem: it outperforms state-of-the-art DG methods that were developed using large models with a large margin. Moreover, we observe that the teacher-student performance gap on test data with domain shift is bigger than that on in-distribution data. To improve DG for tiny neural networks without increasing the deployment cost, we propose a simple idea called out-of-distribution knowledge distillation (OKD), which aims to teach the student how the teacher handles (synthetic) out-of-distribution data and is proved to be a promising framework for tackling the problem. We also contribute a scalable method for creating DG datasets, called DOmain Shift in COntext (DOSCO), which can be applied to broad data at scale without much human effort. Code and models will be released.
